content: 1. Patients who are traced shortly after missing a visit are more likely to re-engage in care compared to those who experience a prolonged period of disengagement. 2. The Guidelines Development Group has identified eight strategies to enhance access to and delivery of high-quality health services for individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). These strategies build upon the simplified service delivery models established in 2018 for HIV and hepatitis C care, which are also applicable to CHB management. 3. These strategies aim to support the implementation of key recommendations for expanding hepatitis B treatment eligibility and improving access to effective testing, treatment, and care. Emphasis is placed on promoting long-term adherence and retention in care, as most individuals with CHB require lifelong antiviral therapy. 4. The eight approaches are expected to evolve into formal recommendations as comparative studies are conducted and a robust evidence base specific to hepatitis B is established. 5. Barriers to successful uptake of testing and linkage to care, treatment, and prevention for CHB include individual factors (e.g., mental health issues, substance abuse, misinformation, depression, lack of social or family support, and fear of disclosure) and structural or economic factors (e.g., stigma, discrimination, high costs of care, distance from care sites, transportation costs, and long waiting times). 6. Effective interventions to expand testing uptake and improve linkage to confirmatory viral load testing and treatment include the use of dried blood spots for serological and virological testing, peer and lay health worker support in community-based settings, electronic reminders and clinician prompts for facility-based testing, and integrating testing into broader health services. 7. The 2017 WHO guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing recommend adopting strategies to enhance testing uptake and linkage to care, including peer and lay health worker support, clinician reminders for provider-initiated testing, integrated testing services, and the use of dried blood spot specimens for nucleic acid testing (NAT) and serology. 8. Additional interventions to promote linkage include on-site rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) with same-day results, reflex laboratory-based virological NAT of positive serology samples, and providing transportation assistance for patients who need to travel long distances to treatment centers. 9. Suboptimal adherence to antiviral therapy is a significant challenge in achieving sustained suppression of HBV DNA viral load, reducing disease progression, and preventing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and death. Factors contributing to poor adherence include forgetfulness, changes in daily routine, depression, substance misuse, and stigma. 10. While specific adherence support strategies for long-term CHB care are lacking, principles from effective long-term antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence support for HIV can be applied to CHB care. These include peer counseling, mobile phone text reminders, cognitive behavioral therapy, behavioral skills training, and simplified medication regimens. 11. Retention in care and re-engagement of patients who have disengaged from CHB care are critical challenges. Factors influencing disengagement include male sex, lower educational status, poor adherence, non-disclosure, distance from clinics, and lack of understanding of the need for lifelong care. 12. Evidence-based interventions from HIV care to trace and re-engage patients include remote communication (phone, text messages, mail, email), in-person tracing, and community-based interventions such as patient advocates, peer support, and adherence clubs. 13. Integrating hepatitis B testing, care, and treatment with existing health services can improve access and efficiency. This includes providing testing in antenatal clinics, ART clinics, TB clinics, and sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics, as well as integrating CHB diagnosis with existing diagnostic platforms and laboratory services. 14. Integrated service delivery for hepatitis B care can leverage existing HIV or primary care services to increase access, particularly for high-risk populations such as people who inject drugs. This approach also facilitates shared reporting systems and better coordination of care. 15. Decentralizing hepatitis B services to peripheral health facilities and community-based venues can bring care closer to patients, reduce transportation costs, and improve linkage to treatment and follow-up. This approach has been successful in scaling up HIV and hepatitis C care in lowand middle-income countries. 16. Task sharing, which involves delegating care responsibilities to non-specialist healthcare workers, is a pragmatic solution to address shortages of trained healthcare professionals. This approach has been widely adopted in HIV care and is now recommended for hepatitis C care as well. 17. Differentiated care for hepatitis B involves tailoring services to meet the needs of patients with complex conditions requiring specialized care while alleviating the burden on centralized clinics. This client-centered approach simplifies and adapts service delivery across the care continuum.
